title: Part VII — PLATFORMS: Paying Many Parties

know: The three questions every platform payment answers (who is the merchant, whose balance holds the money, who carries the loss) and where each provider records the answer: Stripe in an account's responsibilities and the charge type, Adyen in the account structure, the liable balance account and each payment's split instructions.
That seller verification is a state the provider reopens for the life of the account, and that payouts are usually the first thing to stop when a requirement passes its deadline.
How one payment is divided and paid out on each provider, and what happens to a refund or chargeback that arrives after the seller was paid.
Which accounts, cards and financing products each provider offers to a platform's sellers as of November 2026, at which release stage, and under which license.
believe: Choosing an account model is choosing who pays when a seller cannot; it is not an integration detail.
A platform that never holds funds can still carry the loss on them.
can_do: For a described platform business, say who the merchant is, which account and charge configuration follows on each provider, and whose balance a chargeback debits.
Design the platform's own records for sellers: the liability decisions per account, the verification requirements and deadlines, a ledger entry per leg of a split, and an exposure figure per seller.
Judge a proposal to add accounts, cards or financing by license, country, release stage and the duties it adds to the platform.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one chapter, and every chapter supports at least one.
Each chapter's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.
Given a platform business the part does not contain, a reader of Part VII alone says who carries a seller's unrecoverable chargebacks and names the earlier decision that settled it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A tutoring marketplace charges parents under its own name and pays tutors every Friday. One tutor collects €9,000 in prepaid lessons, is paid out, and disappears; the parents' banks reverse the payments (chargebacks). Using only Part VII: who ends up paying the €9,000, what decided that, and what number should the marketplace have been tracking?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The marketplace pays. Parents understand they are buying from the marketplace, so it is the merchant and the payments are booked through its own balance at the provider; chargebacks debit that balance (the platform balance on Stripe, the liable balance account on Adyen), and it can recover only what the tutor's balance or bank account still yields. The decision was the account and charge model chosen at the start, not anything done at dispute time. The number is exposure per seller: volume already paid out that can still be refunded or disputed.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of Part VII can list what a platform must check before offering sellers a card or a stored balance, without assuming the product is available wherever the platform takes payments.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A platform that takes payments in the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and the United States wants to give its sellers a debit card that spends their sales balance. Name the questions it must answer, per provider and per country, before it promises a launch date.
acceptance_criteria.expected: Which licensed institution issues the card and holds the balance (the provider's own bank license or a partner bank); whether the product is available in each country and at which release stage (generally available, preview, in development), with the date of that information; whether the platform's current account model qualifies (on Stripe, as documented, the platform must bear seller losses); what extra verification sellers must pass; and who answers each card authorization within the two-second window and what the default is when the platform does not answer.

thesis.question: What does a platform take on when it puts itself between a payer and a seller?
thesis.claim: A platform takes on its sellers' unpaid refunds, chargebacks and negative balances, and the work of keeping those sellers verified, to the extent its account model assigns them to it; it makes that assignment when it configures accounts and payments, long before the first loss, and not holding the funds does not undo it.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the account model is an integration and user-experience choice (which dashboard sellers see, how sign-up looks, which API calls are made), and that liability is a contract question legal can settle afterwards, since the provider holds the license and the money.
thesis.so_what: A platform team that accepts the claim decides who bears seller losses first and derives onboarding, the split and the product plan from that; it stops reading 'we never hold the funds' as 'we never carry the loss', and it keeps its own figure for how much paid-out money can still come back.
thesis.how_why: Card-network rules decide who the merchant is by what the cardholder sees and who gives recourse, and both providers turn that into configuration. Stripe's documentation (n.d., accessed November 2026) fixes an account's fee and loss responsibilities when it is configured as a merchant and does not let them be changed; negative transactions follow the charge type to the seller's or the platform's balance. Adyen's documentation (n.d., accessed November 2026) books everything to the platform's liable balance account unless split instructions say otherwise and debits that account when a seller's balance goes negative. The same assignment decides who collects verification data, where a refund after payout lands, and whether accounts and cards may be offered at all. Adyen documents an arrangement in which it bears seller losses only as a pilot with limited availability (Managed Risk), so on that point the comparison is between Stripe's standing per-account option and an Adyen pilot.

supporting_claims.claim: Who the customer understands they are buying from decides who the merchant is; the account and charge configuration must follow that fact, and it fixes whose balance refunds and chargebacks debit and who stands behind a seller's negative balance.

Seller verification is a state the provider reopens for as long as the account lives, and a platform that treats it as a sign-up form finds out through stopped payouts; who collects the data follows from who bears the losses.

A split is provisional because sellers are paid before the refund and dispute window closes: a reversal after payout is funded by the platform whenever the payment was booked through it, so the platform's exposure is the paid-out volume that can still come back.

Accounts, cards and financing for sellers reach only as far as a license or partner bank does, are offered at different release stages per country, and add duties to the platform; on Stripe, as documented, only a platform that already bears seller losses may offer accounts and cards.

role.contribution: Shows that the gap between the instant answer and the slow truth gets a third party to carry it once a platform sits between payer and seller, and that the platform chooses how much of it to carry when it picks its account model.

additional_patterns.applies_to: platform-onboarding-and-verification to embedded-finance: a seller is admitted, then paid, then offered more than payments

flow.rationale: The model chapter fixes who the merchant is and who bears losses. On Stripe that decision determines who collects verification data, so onboarding cannot be explained before it. A seller must hold an active capability before any payment can be split to it, so onboarding precedes splits. Embedded finance comes last because its products sit on the seller balance the splits chapter defines and, on Stripe, require the loss assignment the first chapter explains. If splits came first, the reader would watch a refund debit the platform's balance with no reason for it; if embedded finance came earlier, its preconditions would be terms the reader has not met.

hook.content: On 18 March 2027 Mila Janssen asks for €84.00 back for the seven classes she has not used on her €120 pass. Studio Noord was paid its €117.47 a week earlier, on Thursday 11 March. Mila will get her €84.00; the open question is whose balance it comes out of today, and that was decided long before she asked.

opening.bridge: From the two-party payments of Parts I to VI, where the business that takes the payment is the business that owes the refund, to a platform such as Larkfield, which is not the seller, never holds the money, and can still be the one that pays.
opening.roadmap: Four chapters in the order a platform meets the questions: who is the merchant and who carries the loss; how sellers are verified and kept verified; how one payment is divided, paid out and reversed; and what it takes to offer sellers accounts, cards and financing.

closing.synthesis: The four chapters describe one decision seen four times. Who stands behind a seller's negative balance decides who the provider lets collect verification data, where a refund after payout is booked, and whether the platform may offer accounts and cards at all. A platform that picks its account model for the look of its onboarding has picked its loss exposure, its operational workload and the limit of its product plan in the same act.
closing.so_what: Before adding sellers, countries or financial products, a platform can state its position in one line per provider: who is the merchant, who bears negative balances, who collects requirements, where reversals after payout are booked. If it cannot, it is carrying a liability it has not measured.
closing.callback: Mila's €84.00 refund a week after Studio Noord's payout: the reader can now say which balance funded it on each provider and why, and what Larkfield would need in place before letting studios spend that same balance on a card.

takeaway.content: Write down, per provider, the four answers (merchant, loss bearer, requirements collector, where reversals after payout are booked), mirror every seller's requirements and deadlines with an owner, and track exposure per seller, before launching any product that keeps or lends seller money.

transition_in.carries_over: Part VI's billing machinery and its last chapter's question of who sells to the customer, answered there by letting the provider sell in its own name (merchant of record).
transition_in.introduces: The opposite arrangement: the seller stays the seller, a platform stands between it and the payer, and the liability, of which a merchant of record takes over only the part its contract names, is now divided among three parties by the account model.

posts.title: Part VII — PLATFORMS: Paying Many Parties
posts.question: What does Part VII argue, and in what order should its chapters be read?

know: Part VII argues that a platform's account model is its liability model, and answers four questions in order: who is the merchant and who carries the loss, how sellers are verified, how a payment is divided and paid out, and what accounts, cards and financing require.
believe: A platform that never holds funds can still be the party that pays for a refund or a chargeback.
can_do: Pick the Part VII chapter that answers the platform decision in front of them.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can state the part's claim and name the four chapters' subjects in reading order.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only this page: what does Part VII argue, and what will each of its four chapters tell you, in order?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The account model a platform chooses decides who pays when a seller cannot. Then: platform models (merchant, money, loss); onboarding and verification of sellers; splits, seller balances and payouts, including a refund after payout; accounts, cards and financing for sellers.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The page opens with Mila's €84.00 refund request of 18 March 2027 after Studio Noord's payout of 11 March, with amounts and dates as in the scenario ledger, and leaves the question of who funds it open for the chapters.

role.contribution: Performs the part's opening: poses the refund-after-payout question, states the part thesis and gives the reading order.

posts.title: One Payment, Three Parties: Platform and Marketplace Models
posts.question: When a platform sits between payer and seller, who is the merchant, who holds the money and who carries the loss?

know: What a payment facilitator, a sponsored merchant and a marketplace are in card-network rules, and why most platforms use a provider's platform product instead of registering as a facilitator.

Stripe Connect's charge types and the responsibilities an account carries, and Adyen for Platforms' resources (legal entity, account holder, balance account, liable balance account), as answers to the same three questions.

What each provider documents about negative seller balances, and that Adyen documents the platform as the default bearer, a 30-day negative-balance period, and a Managed Risk pilot in which Adyen bears seller losses.
believe: Who bears seller losses is the first decision of a platform integration, because the other settings depend on it and on Stripe it cannot be changed on an existing account.
can_do: Given a platform business, name the merchant from what the customer sees, choose the matching configuration on each provider, and say whose balance a chargeback debits and who stands behind it.
Translate a statement made in one provider's platform vocabulary into the other's, and say where the two do not map one to one.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a platform business the chapter does not contain, the reader identifies the merchant from what the customer sees, not from the API calls, and derives the configuration and the loss bearer on both providers.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A booking tool for dog groomers lets a customer book and pay a named groomer; the groomer's name is on the card statement and the tool keeps 3%. Using only this chapter: who is the merchant, which kind of charge or account setup fits on Stripe and on Adyen, and if a customer's bank reverses a payment (a chargeback) after the groomer has closed the business, who pays?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The groomer is the merchant, because the customer understands they are buying from the groomer. On Stripe that means a direct charge, or a charge through the platform that names the groomer as the business of record; on Adyen the platform model, in which the shopper deals directly with the platform's user. The chargeback debits the groomer's balance on a Stripe direct charge, and if that balance stays negative the loss goes to whoever was assigned negative-balance responsibility when the account was configured (Stripe or the tool). On Adyen it debits the tool's liable balance account by default unless the payment's chargeback instructions name the groomer's balance account, and by default the liable account stands behind a negative seller balance (Adyen's Managed Risk pilot is the documented exception).

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every Stripe and Adyen statement about liability carries its source and date, and the chapter says in plain words that Adyen's default puts the platform behind its sellers and that Adyen bearing seller losses is documented only as a pilot with limited availability (Managed Risk).

The terms the rest of Part VII relies on (connected account, charge type, balance platform, account holder, balance account, liable account, negative balance) are each defined here in one sentence before they are used.

thesis.question: When a platform sits between payer and seller, who is the merchant, who holds the money and who carries the loss?
thesis.claim: The merchant is whoever the customer understands they are buying from, the money sits in balances at the provider and not with the platform, and the loss falls first on the balance the payment was booked to and then on the party assigned to cover that balance when it goes negative. The platform's configuration does not decide who the merchant is, but it must agree with it, and it does decide the booking and the loss bearer, on Stripe permanently for each account.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that Standard, Express and Custom accounts, or marketplace and platform setups, differ in how much user interface the platform builds, so the choice belongs to the product team and can be revisited when the business model changes.
thesis.so_what: A team should settle who bears seller losses before it designs onboarding or the checkout, record that decision per account in its own systems, and expect a change of commercial model on Stripe to mean new accounts for its sellers, not a changed setting.
thesis.how_why: Visa's rules (October 2026 edition) classify an entity as the merchant if it sells to the cardholder, is named to the cardholder and gives recourse in a dispute. Stripe's documentation (n.d., accessed November 2026) tells platforms to determine the merchant of record from the business model and not from the charge type, books negative transactions to the seller's balance for direct charges and to the platform's for charges made through the platform, offers a setting under which Stripe is responsible for negative seller balances, and says of an account's fee and loss responsibilities that their values cannot be updated later. Adyen's documentation (n.d., accessed November 2026) books amounts and fees to the platform's liable balance account unless split instructions say otherwise and deducts from it when sellers' balance accounts go negative. Where they differ, as documented in 2026: Stripe exposes loss bearing as a per-account choice with Stripe as one option; Adyen puts the platform behind its sellers by default and documents, as a pilot with limited availability, a Managed Risk programme in which Adyen bears seller losses.

role.contribution: Establishes the three questions, the two vocabularies and the loss assignment that the other three chapters build on.

transition_in.carries_over: The part intro's open question: Studio Noord has been paid, Mila wants €84.00 back, and someone's balance must fund it.
transition_in.introduces: The answer in general form: who the merchant is, whose balance holds the money and who stands behind that balance, stated in Stripe's and in Adyen's terms.

posts.title: Letting Sellers In: Onboarding and Verification on Platforms
posts.question: How does a platform get thousands of small businesses verified without losing them or its licence partner's trust?

know: What a capability and a verification requirement are, and how each provider reports what is missing and by when: Stripe as lists of requirements with a per-account deadline, Adyen as a per-capability allowed flag with standard deadlines of 30 or 60 days.
The events that reopen verification after sign-up: changed seller data, changed rules, volume thresholds and periodic reviews.
The three ways to collect verification data (provider-hosted, embedded components, the platform's own forms over the API) and what each leaves the platform to maintain.
That neither company publishes a completion rate or a comparison of its onboarding flows; the one public figure is a 2019 Stripe claim about a redesign.
believe: Verification is a state with deadlines and an owner, not a form completed once.
Collecting sellers' documents itself is work a platform should take on only when it has also chosen to carry their losses.
can_do: Diagnose a seller's stopped payouts from requirement and capability state, and say what the platform should have stored and surfaced to prevent it.
Choose between hosted, embedded and API onboarding for a stated platform, naming what the platform must then keep up to date.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a seller complaint the chapter does not contain, the reader explains it from verification state and names the records and the owner that would have prevented it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A seller on your platform writes: 'Customers can still pay me, but my payouts stopped on Monday and nobody told me why.' Using only this chapter: what most likely happened, why did payouts stop while payments continued, and what should the platform have had in place?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A verification requirement was reopened (changed data, a new rule, a threshold or a periodic review) and its deadline passed. Payouts go first: Stripe documents that it typically disables payouts at the deadline and charges only later, and Adyen's standard deadline is 30 days for payout capabilities against 60 for receiving payments. The platform should mirror each seller's open requirements, deadlines and capability status from the provider, give every deadline an owner, remind the seller through a monitored channel, and show the seller the reason and the provider's link or component to fix it.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a proposal to build onboarding forms on the API, the reader names what the platform takes on that a hosted flow would have carried.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Your product team wants its own sign-up forms for sellers, sending the data to the provider by API, to keep the brand consistent. Using only this chapter, name two things the platform takes on by doing so.
acceptance_criteria.expected: Any two of: keeping the forms current when requirements change (Stripe documents that API onboarding needs integration changes and a review at least every six months, while hosted and embedded flows update immediately); handling sellers' identity documents itself; supporting each new country and business type by hand; and, on Stripe, a configuration in which the platform collects requirements only if it also bears seller losses.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The chapter states that no completion rate or comparison of onboarding flows is public for either provider, and presents the one published figure (Stripe, 2019) as a dated vendor claim.

thesis.question: How does a platform get thousands of small businesses verified without losing them or its licence partner's trust?
thesis.claim: By treating verification as a state the provider reopens for the life of every account, not as a sign-up step. To keep sellers, the platform requests only the capabilities a seller needs and lets the provider's hosted or embedded flow collect the documents; to keep the trust of the licensed provider, whose license requires the checks, it mirrors every open requirement and deadline with a named owner, so that the seller hears of a missing document from the platform first and the provider does not have to restrict an account the platform had not noticed.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that onboarding is a conversion funnel that ends at sign-up, so the platform should own every screen through the API to keep drop-off low, and can leave what happens afterwards to the provider's emails to the seller.
thesis.so_what: Verification becomes an operated system with an owner, alerts and a seller-facing explanation, not a project that ends at launch: the first thing a neglected requirement breaks is a seller's payout, the first place it shows is the support queue, and because neither provider publishes a completion rate or a comparison of flows the platform has to measure sign-up drop-off on its own flows.
thesis.how_why: Both providers gate what a seller may do behind capabilities that depend on verification, and both reopen verification after sign-up. Adyen's documentation (n.d., accessed November 2026) names the events that trigger verification, among them a seller changing its data and periodic data reviews, and standard deadlines of 30 days for payout capabilities and 60 for receiving payments; Stripe's (n.d., accessed November 2026) lists requirements as currently due, eventually due and past due against a per-account deadline and says it typically disables payouts first. That is the documented difference: Adyen's deadlines are standard periods a platform can build reminders on, Stripe's must be read per account. Stripe also documents that its hosted and embedded flows pick up new requirements immediately while API onboarding needs integration changes, and that who collects requirements is derived from who bears losses. Neither company publishes a completion rate or a comparison of its flows, so the cost of a hosted flow in lost sign-ups cannot be stated from the public record.

role.contribution: Shows the first consequence of the loss assignment: the provider's license requires every seller to be verified continuously, and the platform inherits the deadlines whether or not it collects the data.

transition_in.carries_over: Chapter 33's result that every seller is an account at a licensed provider, with someone standing behind its losses.
transition_in.introduces: What follows from that: the provider must know who each seller is before the account may take payments or receive payouts, and must keep knowing it, which makes verification a state with deadlines.

posts.title: Dividing the Money: Splits, Platform Balances and Seller Payouts
posts.question: How is one payment divided among platform, seller and provider, and how does each get paid?

know: How a payment is divided on each provider: on Stripe an application fee or later transfers between balances, depending on the charge type; on Adyen a list of typed split instructions sent with the payment or applied from a store's profile.
Who pays the processing fee in each setup, and why on Adyen some fees are not known when the payment is made.
What a refund and a chargeback do to a payment that was already split and paid out, and the tools for recovering the seller's share.
How seller payouts are scheduled on each provider and what a top-up is.
believe: A split is not final when the seller is paid; it is final when the payment can no longer be refunded or disputed.
'Payment succeeded' does not prove 'seller credited'; only reconciling each leg does.
can_do: Write the ledger entries for one split payment, its payout and a later refund, keyed so the refund finds the bookings it must unwind.
Say, for a refund or chargeback after payout, whose balance is debited first and how the platform recovers the seller's share.
Compute a per-seller exposure figure from paid-out volume and the refund and dispute windows.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a split payment the chapter does not contain, refunded after the seller was paid, the reader says who is out of pocket if the seller cannot repay and what record the platform needed in order to unwind the split.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A marketplace charges a buyer €200 through its own account at the provider, keeps €20 and credits the seller €180, which is paid out to the seller's bank on Friday. On Monday the buyer is refunded in full. The seller's balance at the provider is empty and the seller does not answer. Using only this chapter: who has paid for the refund so far, how can the marketplace try to get the €180 back, and what must it have recorded on Friday to do so?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The marketplace has paid: the refund debits the balance the payment was booked through (the platform balance on Stripe, the liable balance account on Adyen, which also stands behind a seller balance that goes negative). It can reverse the seller's share so that the seller's balance turns negative and is refilled from future sales, or debit the seller's bank account where the seller consented. It needed a record linking the charge to each leg of the split (seller share, platform fee, provider fee, payout), so that the refund can find what to reverse.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can explain why an approved payment on Adyen does not prove that the seller was credited, and name what to reconcile.
acceptance_criteria.probe: On Adyen, a payment with split instructions is approved. Using only this chapter: can the platform conclude that the seller's balance account was credited? Why or why not, and what should it check?
acceptance_criteria.expected: No. Adyen documents that the payment request validates only the format of the split instructions; if the named balance account does not exist or its account holder is closed, the whole amount and its fees are booked to the platform's liable balance account without an error. The platform should reconcile the bookings per split (transfer webhooks or the accounting report) against its own ledger.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The worked example splits Mila's €120.00 into €117.47 for Studio Noord and a €2.53 Larkfield fee, with the €0.61 provider cost labeled as an assumption, and the refund of €84.00 on 18 March 2027 follows the payout of 11 March, all as in the scenario ledger.

thesis.question: How is one payment divided among platform, seller and provider, and how does each get paid?
thesis.claim: A payment is divided by booking parts of it to balances inside the provider: the seller's share to the seller's balance, the platform's fee to the platform's, and the provider's fee deducted from whichever of the two the configuration names; seller and platform are then paid by later payouts from their balances. Because sellers are paid before the refund and dispute window closes, the division is provisional: a refund or chargeback after payout is funded by the platform whenever the payment was booked through it, and the platform must then recover the seller's share itself.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a split is arithmetic done once at payment time (compute the fee, send the rest), that a refund runs the same arithmetic backwards, and that the provider keeps the parties square.
thesis.so_what: The platform needs a ledger entry for every leg of a split, keyed so a refund can find what to reverse, a per-seller figure for paid-out volume that can still come back, and a reconciliation that checks each seller was credited; a platform that only tracks 'paid' discovers the shortfall later, as an unexplained difference between its own ledger and the provider's balances.
thesis.how_why: On Stripe the division is a set of movements between the platform's and the seller's balances that follows the charge type; on Adyen it is a list of typed split instructions declared with the payment. Stripe's documentation (n.d., accessed November 2026) moves the full amount of a destination charge to the seller and the application fee back to the platform, debits the platform's balance for a refund or dispute on a charge made through the platform, and leaves recovery to a transfer reversal the platform requests; a direct charge debits the seller's balance instead. Adyen's (n.d., accessed November 2026) takes a splits list with types for the seller's share, the commission and each fee, calculates transaction fees after the payment, allows a refund to be deducted only from the balance accounts that were credited, and has the platform choose where a chargeback will be booked when it sends the payment. Two documented differences matter to an integrator: Adyen fixes the chargeback booking at payment time where Stripe leaves the reversal to dispute time, and a split naming a missing or closed balance account is booked to the liable account without an error on Adyen, where a Stripe transfer fails. Each company has published a general account of its internal ledger; how either books a platform's splits and transfers in it is not public.

role.contribution: Turns the loss assignment into money movements: shows where each euro of a payment is booked, when it leaves the provider, and whose balance funds a reversal that arrives afterwards.

transition_in.carries_over: A verified seller whose capabilities to take payments and receive transfers are active, so its payouts can run.
transition_in.introduces: The first payment to that seller: how it is divided among three parties, when each is paid, and what a reversal after payout does to the division.

posts.title: Beyond Payments: Accounts, Cards and Capital as Platform Features
posts.question: What does it take to offer accounts, cards and loans to a platform's sellers, and how far have the two providers gone?

know: What banking-as-a-service, a financial account, card issuing and financing repaid from processed volume are, in plain words.
Which license stands behind each product: Adyen's own banking licenses, and Stripe's money-transmission and e-money licenses with named partner banks and lenders.
The stated availability of each product as of November 2026, by country and release stage, including what is in preview or in development.
That issuing puts the platform in the card authorization path with a two-second window on both providers.
believe: Embedded finance is not switched on where payments already run; it is a separate decision per product, per country and per release stage.
Each product that keeps, spends or lends seller money adds duties to the platform even though the provider holds the license.
can_do: Assess a proposal to offer sellers an account, a card or financing by license, country, release stage, preconditions on the platform's account model and the duties added.
State what happens to card payments when the platform's authorization endpoint does not answer, and choose the default deliberately.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a product plan the chapter does not contain, the reader lists the checks to make per provider and per country and treats the chapter's availability facts as dated.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A platform with sellers in Germany and the United States wants to let them keep their sales in an account at the provider instead of being paid out to their bank, starting next quarter. Using only this chapter: what must it check on Stripe and on Adyen before promising that date, and what would you say about how current the chapter's own answer is?
acceptance_criteria.expected: On each provider: whether an account product for platform users is available in each country and at which stage (as of November 2026, Stripe's current platform product was in preview, with a US legacy version not open to new builds, and Adyen described business accounts as in development); which licensed institution holds the funds; the preconditions (on Stripe the platform must bear seller losses; on Adyen the feature is enabled per balance platform, with extra verification and Adyen's authentication SDK for outgoing transfers); and what the platform must now run (statements, authentication, fraud controls). The reader adds that these stages are dated November 2026 and must be checked again.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what a provider does when the platform does not answer a card authorization in time.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Your platform issues cards to sellers and approves each purchase from its own server. That server is unreachable for ten minutes. Using only this chapter: what happens to purchases made on those cards during that time?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Each authorization waits up to two seconds for the platform's answer (2 seconds on Stripe, 2,000 milliseconds on Adyen, as documented); with no answer the provider applies the default the platform configured in advance, approve or decline. The platform therefore decided the outcome when it set the default, and its endpoint needs its own availability target.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every availability statement names its release stage and country and is dated; nothing in preview, pilot or development is described as available.

The chapter's conclusion synthesizes Part VII (one loss assignment seen in the model, verification, the split and financial products) and returns to Mila's €84.00 refund after payout before handing off to Part VIII.

thesis.question: What does it take to offer accounts, cards and loans to a platform's sellers, and how far have the two providers gone?
thesis.claim: It takes a licensed institution behind each product, and that license covers the product, not the platform's operating duties: the platform must answer each card authorization within two seconds and accept what the provider attaches, which is added seller verification on Adyen and bearing seller losses on Stripe. Neither provider has reached a feature switch: as of November 2026 availability differs by product, country and release stage, and accounts for a platform's sellers are in preview at Stripe and in development at Adyen.
thesis.disputed_by: The view, encouraged by provider descriptions such as Adyen's 'within a single integration' (H1 2026 shareholder letter), that a platform already taking payments can add accounts, cards and loans as features wherever it operates, with the provider carrying the regulated part.
thesis.so_what: A platform plans these products per country and per release stage, checks whether its account model qualifies before it promises anything, and treats a card or account launch as taking on operating duties of a financial product; declining to launch, as Larkfield, the book's fictional platform, does with its instant-payout card, is a legitimate result of that assessment.
thesis.how_why: Adyen's H1 2026 shareholder letter attributes its accounts, issuing and capital products to its own banking licenses, and its statements carry merchant funds in business accounts and loans on its own balance sheet. Stripe's documentation (n.d., accessed November 2026) says Stripe is not a bank and names partner banks for deposits, cards and loans and third-party lenders outside the United States. That is the documented difference: one licensed balance sheet extended across products, against products assembled per country from partners. On Stripe a platform for which Stripe bears seller losses cannot use Treasury or Issuing, which ties these products to the loss assignment of chapter 33; on Adyen they are enabled per balance platform with added capabilities and verification. Both give the platform about two seconds to approve a card authorization before a configured default applies. As of November 2026 both offer card issuing and financing in named countries; Stripe's current account product for platforms is in public preview in the United Kingdom and private preview in the United States, Australia and the EU (and, on one page, Canada), with a US legacy version closed to new builds, and Adyen's business accounts are documented as in development. The public record gives no date for general availability of either company's account product, so the chapter reports stages as of November 2026 and stops there.

role.contribution: Tests the part's claim at its far end: the products built on the seller balance are gated by license and by the platform's loss assignment; also carries the part's closing.

transition_in.carries_over: The seller balance of chapter 35, which exists between the split and the payout and is emptied on a schedule.
transition_in.introduces: What a platform can offer if that money stays, is spent or is advanced (an account, a card, financing), and what each requires of the provider's license and of the platform.
